slides.section: Opening: the AI sprawl problem in IT terms
slides.eyebrow: The Smarter Project · For IT leadership
slides.title: One control plane for enterprise AI

body.text: A self-hosted, open-source platform for building, running and governing AI applications as declared, auditable resources.

slides.notes: About 1 minute. Set expectations: this is the big-picture technical view, organized around the four people in the room: the CIO, the head of application development, the head of infrastructure, and the head of technical support. Each gets a section. We’ll start with the problem in IT terms, then the architecture, then each role, and finish with what is still missing and a 90-day pilot.

slides.section: Opening: the AI sprawl problem in IT terms
slides.title: AI sprawl is now an IT problem

body.text: Provider API keys copied into apps, laptops and CI pipelines, with no central rotation or revocation.
Each team builds its own retrieval, agent and tool-calling code, with its own bugs and its own security review.
Token spend lands on one vendor invoice, with no breakdown by user, team or application, and no hard limits.
Nobody can reconstruct what a model was sent, which tools it called, or what it returned.

slides.notes: About 2 minutes. Describe the pattern most IT organizations are living through. AI adoption started bottom-up: individual teams got API keys and built what they needed. The result looks like the early days of cloud before landing zones: credentials scattered, duplicated platforms, a cost line nobody can break down, and nothing an auditor can follow. Ask the room which of the four they recognize. Usually it is all four.

slides.section: The big picture: architecture and the declarative resource model
slides.title: A self-hosted control plane where every AI capability, from a model key to a guardrail, is a declared resource with an owner, a budget and an audit trail.
slides.notes: About 1 minute. If they remember one sentence, it should be this one. The comparison that lands with IT audiences: Smarter does for AI what Kubernetes did for compute. You declare the desired state of a resource in a manifest, the platform reconciles it, and everything it runs is inventoried and governed. The business sees an AI resource management system; IT sees a control plane.

slides.section: The big picture: architecture and the declarative resource model
slides.title: Architecture at a glance

body.text: Access & governance · accounts, secrets, budgets, proxy
Extensibility & trust · tools, MCP, RAG, guardrails
OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, DeepSeek; self-hosted via vLLM or Ollama
SQL databases, REST APIs, MCP servers, web search, documents

slides.notes: About 3 minutes. Walk left to right. On the left, every way people and programs reach Smarter: the web console, the CLI and VS Code extension, a REST API with a published OpenAPI document, SDKs in three languages, an embeddable React chat component, and, through the Proxy, the vendors’ own SDKs unchanged. In the middle, the platform, organized as four resource layers. Underneath it is a conventional, supportable stack: Django and Django REST Framework, Celery workers for asynchronous work, MariaDB, Redis, all containerized and run on Kubernetes. On the right, everything Smarter brokers access to: commercial model vendors, self-hosted open models, and your own systems. The architectural point: all traffic between people and models, and between models and your systems, passes through one governed layer.

slides.section: The big picture: architecture and the declarative resource model
slides.title: Everything is a declared resource

rows: Account, User, Secret, Budget, Proxy, API key
Provider, LLMHost, LLMClient, Orchestrator, Custom Domain
Plugin (API, SQL, web search, skill), Connection, MCPClient, Vectorstore, Guardrail
Prompt: history, tool calls, guardrail results, cost

body.text: Each resource has an owner and an account, is created from a manifest, and is managed through one API.

slides.notes: About 2 minutes. This is the idea behind the phrase “AI resources.” Every capability in Smarter is a typed resource, the way a Kubernetes cluster has Deployments, Services and Secrets. The layers matter for governance: Access and Governance resources set the boundaries; everything else operates inside them. And they map naturally onto your organization: infrastructure and security own the top layer, developers mostly work in the middle, and support and analysts work with the conversation records at the bottom. Because every Prompt links back through the guardrails, tools and model that produced it to the account and budget that authorized it, the whole stack is auditable end to end.

slides.section: The big picture: architecture and the declarative resource model
slides.title: Infrastructure as code, for AI

body.text:
apiVersion: smarter.sh/v1
kind: LLMClient
metadata:
  name: hr_policy_assistant
spec:
  config:
    prompt:
      provider: openai
      defaultModel: gpt-6-luna
  plugins:
    - hr_policy_search
  guardrails:
    - pii_redaction_input
    - prompt_injection_llm_judge_input
    - secrets_leak_output

$ smarter apply -f hr-assistant.yaml
$ smarter deploy llmclient hr_policy_assistant
Desired state, not code: the platform does the rest.
Versioned in Git, reviewed in pull requests, applied from CI/CD.
The same file works from the CLI, the API, VS Code or the console.

slides.notes: About 2 minutes. This is the one slide with code, and it is deliberately short. It is an abridged but real-format manifest for an assistant: which model, which tool it may use, and which guardrails screen its input and output. Two commands create it and publish it. For IT, the significance is operational: AI applications become reviewable, diffable configuration that fits your existing change-management process, rather than bespoke code in every team’s repository. For the business, it means a trained analyst can read and change it. The manifest names the plugin and guardrails by reference; those are separate resources, often owned by different people.

slides.section: For the CIO: one control plane, one cost model, no lock-in
slides.title: One platform instead of twenty pilots

body.text: Provider keys live once, encrypted. Teams get revocable Smarter keys instead.
Every request is costed by user, account and application. Budgets in USD or tokens enforce hard stops.
Five commercial vendors and self-hosted models behind one interface. Changing a model is a one-line change.
The same platform teaches AI literacy, with 21 free course designs. The business builds; IT governs.
AGPL-3.0 open source. No license fees or seat counts.

slides.notes: About 2 minutes. Speak to the CIO’s portfolio view. Five things change. Vendor relationships are centralized: provider keys are stored once, in an encrypted vault, and teams use revocable Smarter keys through the Proxy, so rotating a vendor key happens in one place. Spend becomes attributable and capped. Vendor choice becomes reversible. The literacy curriculum turns the business into a source of solutions rather than shadow IT. And there is no license line item; the costs are infrastructure and model usage. On AGPL: running Smarter unmodified carries no source-sharing obligation. If you modify it and let people use the modified version over a network, those users are entitled to your modified source. Have your counsel confirm for your situation.

slides.section: For application development: less code to own, standard integration points
slides.title: Less undifferentiated code to own

body.text: Declared in a manifest, no code
SQL and REST tools, with credentials from Secrets
Any MCP server’s tools; web search; skills
Multi-agent orchestration: sequential, parallel, supervisor/worker, routing, voting
Extensions packaged and shared across teams

slides.notes: About 2 minutes. For the head of custom programming. Most of what teams hand-build today for AI applications is the same plumbing: retrieval, tool calling, credential handling, safety filters and agent coordination. In Smarter that plumbing is platform functionality, configured rather than coded, and tested once for everyone. Your developers’ time moves to the work that is specific to your organization, and to reviewing manifests written by trained business staff, much as they review pull requests today. Note that the platform executes no model-generated code: tools are declared, typed calls, which is also a security property.

slides.section: For application development: less code to own, standard integration points
slides.title: Standard integration points

body.text: Every operation, with a published OpenAPI document and JSON Schemas.
Python, Node.js and Go SDKs; a CLI; a VS Code extension that validates manifests.
Existing OpenAI, Anthropic or Gemini SDK code works unchanged: swap the base URL and key.
A React component and NPM package put an assistant on any web page.
Consume any MCP server’s tools, under the same governance.
Django, DRF and Pydantic, the same framework Smarter is built on, for extensions.

slides.notes: About 2 minutes. The message for development leads: nothing here is proprietary glue. The REST API is fully documented in OpenAPI, so it fits API gateways and client generators. The Proxy is the fastest win: applications already written against a vendor’s SDK keep working, but their keys, spending and logs move under governance by changing two configuration values. MCP support means tools your teams or vendors already expose over the Model Context Protocol plug straight in. And when you do need custom code, it is mainstream Python on Django, not a niche runtime.

slides.section: For infrastructure: deployment, security architecture and model hosting
slides.title: Laptop to Kubernetes, same images

body.text: Evaluation and development on one machine
Production on Kubernetes, published on Artifact Hub
AWS landing zone: EKS, Route 53, ACM, S3, SES
Horizontal autoscaling of app servers and Celery workers
Alpha, beta, next and prod environments in one installation
No managed-service dependency; installs in your existing VPC

slides.notes: About 2 minutes. For the head of infrastructure. The same container images run everywhere, from a laptop under Docker Compose to production Kubernetes under the official Helm chart. For AWS, the project publishes Terraform and Terragrunt modules that build the whole environment, including the EKS cluster, DNS, certificates, storage and email, with remote state in S3. Operationally: app servers and workers scale horizontally, compute can run on spot instances, and one installation separates alpha, beta, next and production environments with clean namespace and resource naming. Be candid that a production install requires real Kubernetes, Terraform and AWS skills; the documentation says so, and recommends a hosting partner for organizations without them.

slides.section: For infrastructure: deployment, security architecture and model hosting
slides.title: Security architecture

body.text: Private subnets for data and compute. HTTPS-only ingress; no SSH needed on EKS. A DNS record and TLS certificate per host, never wildcards.
Encrypted Secret vault. Models never receive credentials, and provider keys are never handed to teams.
Guardrails for PII, secrets, prompt injection, jailbreaks and code injection. Rate limits per user and IP. No execution of model-generated code.
The Smarter Journal persists every API response. Every prompt traces back to its account and budget.

slides.notes: About 3 minutes. This slide will draw the most questions from security-minded attendees. Network: the reference deployment puts the database and compute in private subnets, exposes only HTTPS through the load balancer and ingress, and needs no SSH access to hosts. Each deployed assistant gets its own DNS record and certificate; Smarter deliberately avoids wildcard DNS to prevent subdomain takeover. Credentials: secrets are encrypted at rest and resolved server-side, so neither the model nor the end user ever sees them. Application: deterministic guardrails screen input and output; every API is rate limited (defaults 600 per minute per user, 120 per minute per anonymous IP); custom middleware blocks probing for sensitive files and floods of 404s; and tools are declared, typed calls rather than code execution. Audit: the Journal is designed for long-term, read-optimized storage of every API response. Note the boundaries too: Smarter relies on your cloud for firewalling, WAF, encryption of storage volumes and malware scanning.

slides.section: For infrastructure: deployment, security architecture and model hosting
slides.title: Commercial models, self-hosted models, or both

body.text: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta and DeepSeek. Each provider’s models pass compatibility checks before use, and again periodically.
Your own vLLM or Ollama deployments as managed resources, with provenance, health checks, cost tracking and credentials from Secrets.
Applications see one interface either way. Move a sensitive workload on-premises without changing the application.

slides.notes: About 2 minutes. This answers the data-residency question before it is asked. Commercial vendors are onboarded through a Provider resource, and their models are verified against Smarter’s feature set before teams can use them. For workloads that cannot leave your network, LLMHost registers open models you run yourself, on vLLM, Ollama or another inference stack, with the same governance: health monitoring, cost tracking and secrets handling. Because applications talk to an LLMClient rather than to a vendor, moving a workload between a commercial and a self-hosted model is a configuration change, not a rewrite. Mention that the Provider app’s self-onboarding features are still marked as under active development; the five established providers are stable.

slides.section: For technical support: traceability, cost records and runtime diagnostics
slides.title: Every answer is traceable

body.text: Tokens, model, provider, user and session for every request, in SQL-queryable tables.
Turn on verbose logging for one subsystem from the admin console, with no restart.
Per-user API keys you can revoke, with warnings when a key outlives its maximum age.

slides.notes: About 2 minutes. For the head of technical support. When a user reports that “the AI gave a wrong answer,” support today often has nothing to look at. In Smarter, the prompt record is the starting point of a trace: which assistant answered, which guardrails fired, which tools were called with what results, which model replied, and which account and budget authorized it. Cost accounting is stored per request in ordinary database tables, so chargeback reports are a SQL query. Logging verbosity for a specific subsystem can be switched on at runtime from the admin console. And because every user has their own API keys, a compromised or departing user’s access is revoked individually, without rotating anyone else’s.

slides.section: Maturity, gaps to plan for, and a 90-day pilot
slides.title: Maturity, and the gaps to plan for

body.text: Open source since 2024; release v0.29, pre-1.0
Automated tests in CI, with published coverage
Container images patched at least monthly
Enterprise SSO: Google and GitHub sign-in today; SAML or OIDC needs integration work
Cloud: automated provisioning is AWS only
Support: community and partners; no vendor SLA
Perimeter: WAF, storage encryption and malware scanning come from your cloud

slides.notes: About 2 minutes. Say this before they ask; it builds credibility. Smarter is a real, actively maintained platform, but it is pre-1.0 and community supported. Four things an enterprise should plan for. First, identity: sign-in today is Google or GitHub OAuth plus local accounts. Single sign-on with Okta, Entra ID or another SAML or OIDC provider requires integration work; the authentication backends are configurable, so it is an engineering task rather than a redesign. Second, the Terraform automation targets AWS; on another cloud you supply Kubernetes, DNS and certificates yourself. Third, there is no vendor support desk or SLA; support comes from GitHub, the documentation and hosting partners. Fourth, Smarter relies on your cloud for perimeter controls such as WAF, volume encryption and malware scanning.

slides.section: Maturity, gaps to plan for, and a 90-day pilot
slides.title: A 90-day technical pilot

body.text: Non-production install with Helm on an existing cluster. Route one provider through the Proxy.
A literacy cohort delivers [1–2] business use cases, with one read-only data connection.
Security review against your controls. Cost, usage and audit reports from real traffic.
Production architecture, SSO approach and support model.

slides.notes: About 2 minutes. Each of the four roles has a job in the pilot. Infrastructure stands it up and owns the security review. Application development reviews the manifests and builds the data connection. Technical support uses the prompt records and cost data during the build phase, so it has an informed view by week 12. The CIO gets a decision based on the organization’s own traffic, costs and audit records rather than a vendor’s projections. Routing one existing application through the Proxy in week one is a quick, low-risk way to see cost attribution working before anything new is built. Adjust the timings to the organization.

slides.section: Maturity, gaps to plan for, and a 90-day pilot
slides.title: One control plane for every AI resource
slides.notes: About 1 minute, then questions. Summarize: Smarter replaces a sprawl of keys, one-off stacks and invisible spend with one self-hosted control plane, where every AI capability is a declared, owned, budgeted and audited resource. It fits how IT already works: infrastructure as code, Kubernetes, CI/CD and SQL reporting. Propose the 90-day pilot as the next step, and invite the security and identity questions.
